section-138: In economics a market does not mean only a physical place. It covers any arrangement - by telephone, internet or in person - through which buyers and sellers are in contact and exchange takes place at a price.

Markets are classified by area (local, national, international), by time (very short period, short period, long period) and by competition (perfect competition, monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly). The structure of a market decides how price and output are determined.
section-139: At equilibrium price there is no tendency for price to change because buyers can buy what they want and sellers can sell what they want. If price is higher, excess supply pushes it down; if price is lower, excess demand pushes it up.

An increase in demand raises both equilibrium price and quantity; an increase in supply lowers price and raises quantity. Marshall compared demand and supply to the two blades of a pair of scissors, both necessary to determine price.
section-140: In a perfect market, there is perfect knowledge, perfect mobility of factors, no transport costs and a single uniform price. Imperfect markets include monopoly, monopolistic competition, oligopoly and duopoly, where sellers have some control over price.

Real-world markets are mostly imperfect because of product differentiation, advertising, limited information and barriers to entry. Perfect competition is used as a benchmark to judge the efficiency of other market forms.
section-141: Features: a large number of buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge, perfect mobility and no transport costs. The firm is a price taker, so its demand (AR) curve is horizontal and AR = MR = Price.

Equilibrium: The firm produces where MC = MR and MC cuts MR from below. In the short run it may earn supernormal profit, normal profit or losses. In the long run, free entry and exit eliminate abnormal profits, so the firm earns only normal profit where Price = AR = MR = MC = minimum AC.
section-142: Features: a single seller, no close substitutes and strong barriers to entry such as patents, licences, control of raw materials or economies of scale. The monopolist is a price maker, but cannot fix both price and quantity because demand is determined by buyers.

Equilibrium is at MC = MR. Since the AR curve slopes downward, MR is less than AR, and price is higher than MC. A monopolist may earn supernormal profits even in the long run. Monopoly may lead to higher prices, lower output and exploitation of consumers, so governments regulate it.
section-143: The shutdown point is reached when price equals minimum average variable cost (AVC). If price is above AVC, the firm continues producing even with losses, because it covers variable costs and part of fixed costs. If price falls below AVC, it is better to stop production, since the loss would then be only fixed costs.
In the long run, a firm must cover all costs (price at least equal to minimum AC), otherwise it will leave the industry.
section-144: Accounting profit = total revenue - explicit costs. Economic profit = total revenue - (explicit + implicit costs). Implicit costs include the owner's own capital, labour and land valued at their opportunity cost.

Zero economic profit is called normal profit. It is the minimum return necessary to keep the entrepreneur in the industry. Under perfect competition in the long run, firms earn only normal profit because entry of new firms removes abnormal profits.
section-145: Conditions for price discrimination: (1) the seller must have monopoly power; (2) markets must be separable so that goods cannot be resold from the cheap to the dear market; (3) elasticity of demand must differ across markets.

Examples include different railway fares for different classes, lower fees for students, electricity tariffs for domestic and industrial users and doctors charging rich and poor patients differently. The monopolist charges a higher price where demand is less elastic and a lower price where demand is more elastic.
section-146: First-degree (perfect) discrimination: each unit is sold at the maximum price the buyer is willing to pay, so the seller takes all consumer surplus. Second-degree discrimination: different prices for different quantities or blocks of consumption, such as lower rates for bulk purchase. Third-degree discrimination: the market is divided into groups with different elasticities, such as students and adults or domestic and foreign markets.
These classifications were given by A.C. Pigou. Third-degree discrimination is the most common in practice.
section-147: Controlled prices are fixed by the government, usually below market price, to protect consumers, as in the case of food grains in the Public Distribution System, essential medicines and fertilizers. They may lead to shortages and black markets if supply is inadequate.

Administered prices are fixed by firms or authorities considering costs and policy objectives, such as prices of petroleum products earlier, steel or public utilities. Support prices such as Minimum Support Price (MSP) for crops are fixed to protect farmers.
section-148: The theory was developed by E.H. Chamberlin (1933). Features: many sellers, product differentiation through brand names, packaging and quality, selling costs such as advertising, free entry and exit, and a downward sloping but fairly elastic demand curve.

In the short run firms may earn supernormal profits; in the long run new firms enter and only normal profits remain, with the AR curve tangent to the AC curve. Firms operate with excess capacity because they produce less than the minimum-cost output. Examples include soaps, toothpaste, restaurants and clothing brands.
section-149: Features: few sellers, interdependence of decisions, advertising and selling costs, barriers to entry, possibility of collusion (cartels like OPEC) or price leadership, and indeterminate demand curve because each firm's demand depends on rivals' reactions.
Examples in India include telecom, airlines, automobiles and cement. Models of oligopoly include the kinked demand curve (Sweezy), Cournot's duopoly, cartels, price leadership and game theory.
section-150: The model was developed by Paul Sweezy (1939). If a firm raises its price, rivals do not follow, so it loses many customers; demand above the existing price is elastic. If it cuts its price, rivals follow, so it gains little; demand below the price is inelastic. Hence the demand curve has a kink at the existing price.

This kink creates a gap (discontinuity) in the MR curve. Changes in cost within this gap do not change the profit-maximising output and price, explaining price rigidity. Criticism: it does not explain how the initial price is determined.
section-151: In duopoly, each seller must consider the possible reaction of the other while fixing price or output. Classical models include Cournot's model (each firm assumes the rival's output is fixed), Bertrand's model (firms compete on price) and Edgeworth's model.

If the two firms collude they may act like a monopoly; if they compete fiercely they may come close to the competitive outcome. Examples include two major airlines on a route or two mobile service providers in a region.
section-152: The term was introduced by Joan Robinson. A monopsonist has the power to influence the price at which it buys; for example, a single large factory in a town hiring labour or a sugar mill buying sugarcane from farmers.

Since the monopsonist faces an upward-sloping supply curve, the marginal cost of hiring an extra unit is greater than the price. It hires less and pays lower wages or prices than under competition, leading to exploitation of sellers, such as workers being paid less than their marginal revenue product.
section-153: Example: a single trade union bargaining with a single employer, or a single producer of a raw material selling to a single buyer. Economic theory can show the range within which the price will lie: between the monopolist's preferred higher price and the monopsonist's preferred lower price.
The final price is indeterminate in theory and depends on bargaining strength, negotiation skills, government intervention and alternative options of each party.
section-154: The theory was developed by J.B. Clark, Wicksteed and others. It states that under perfect competition, the price of a factor tends to equal the value of its marginal product (VMP) or marginal revenue product (MRP). A firm employs a factor up to the point where its MRP equals its price.

Assumptions: perfect competition, homogeneous factor units, perfect mobility, full employment and constant technology. Criticism: factors are not homogeneous, perfect competition is rare, marginal product of a single factor is difficult to measure, and it ignores the supply side and trade unions.
section-155: Important theories include the subsistence theory (wages tend to the minimum necessary for survival), the wages-fund theory, the marginal productivity theory, the residual claimant theory and the modern theory of wages, which states that wages are determined by the demand for and supply of labour.

Demand for labour is a derived demand, depending on its productivity and the demand for the final product. Supply depends on population, migration, education and the worker's preference between work and leisure. Trade unions, minimum wage laws and collective bargaining also influence wages.
section-156: Scarcity rent arises because the total supply of land is fixed (perfectly inelastic). When demand increases, the entire price paid for land becomes rent. Even if all land were of equal quality, rent would arise because of scarcity relative to demand.
This is related to the modern theory of rent, which says that any factor earns rent when its supply is less than perfectly elastic. Rent is the surplus over transfer earnings.
section-157: This idea comes from David Ricardo's theory of rent. Ricardo defined rent as 'that portion of the produce of the earth which is paid to the landlord for the use of the original and indestructible powers of the soil'. Land is cultivated in order of fertility; the least fertile land in use is called marginal or no-rent land.

Superior land earns a surplus over the marginal land, which is differential rent. It can arise under extensive cultivation (lands of different fertility) or intensive cultivation (successive doses of labour and capital on the same land). Criticism: there is no fixed order of cultivation and the powers of soil are not indestructible.
section-158: The concept was introduced by Alfred Marshall. Machines, buildings and other capital goods cannot be increased quickly in the short run. If demand rises, their earnings exceed the minimum needed to keep them in use (their variable cost); this surplus is quasi-rent.
Quasi-rent = Total Revenue - Total Variable Cost. In the long run, supply of these factors can be increased, so the surplus disappears. Thus quasi-rent is temporary, unlike pure rent on land.
section-159: According to classical economists such as Marshall and Pigou, interest is the reward for saving (or waiting). The supply of savings increases as the rate of interest rises, while the demand for investment falls as the rate of interest rises. The equilibrium rate of interest is fixed where saving equals investment.

Criticism: It ignores the effect of income on saving, assumes full employment, ignores money and hoarding, and does not explain the interest rate in times of unemployment. Keynes called it indeterminate because saving depends on income, which itself depends on investment.
section-160: Keynes (1936) defined interest as the reward for parting with liquidity for a specified period. Liquidity preference arises from three motives: transactions motive, precautionary motive and speculative motive. The supply of money is fixed by the central bank.

The rate of interest is determined at the point where demand for money (liquidity preference) equals supply of money. If money supply increases, interest falls, but at very low rates the liquidity trap may occur, where people hold any extra money and the interest rate does not fall further.
section-161: This theory was given by Joseph Schumpeter. Innovation means introducing a new product, new method of production, new market, new source of raw material or new organisation. The innovating entrepreneur earns profit until competitors imitate the innovation.
Thus profit is a temporary reward for innovation. The theory explains dynamic change and business cycles, but it ignores risk-bearing and the role of monopoly in profits.
section-162: F.B. Hawley's risk theory states that profit is the reward for risk-bearing; the higher the risk, the higher the profit expected. Frank Knight distinguished between insurable risks (like fire or theft, which can be calculated and insured) and non-insurable uncertainty (like changes in demand, competition or government policy).
According to Knight, profit is the reward for bearing non-insurable uncertainty. This theory is more realistic, though profit may also arise from monopoly and innovation.
section-163: The factors of production are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship, which earn rent, wages, interest and profit respectively. In factor markets, households are sellers and firms are buyers, the opposite of product markets.
Demand for factors is derived demand, depending on the demand for the goods they help produce. The theory of distribution explains how factor prices are determined in these markets.
section-164: Under perfect competition, the factor price is determined by the interaction of industry demand (based on MRP) and supply of the factor. Each firm then employs the factor up to the point where MRP equals the factor price.

Under imperfect competition or monopsony, the factor may be paid less than its marginal revenue product, resulting in exploitation. Trade unions and minimum wage laws can raise wages above the competitive level.
section-165: Welfare economics is a normative branch of economics. It asks questions such as: Is a particular allocation of resources efficient? Does a policy make society better off? How should income be distributed?

Major contributors include Pigou (old welfare economics), Pareto, Kaldor, Hicks, Scitovsky, Bergson and Samuelson (new welfare economics), and Amartya Sen, who emphasised capabilities and social choice.
section-166: A.C. Pigou, in 'The Economics of Welfare' (1920), argued that economic welfare is the part of social welfare that can be measured in money. Welfare increases if national income increases without making the poor worse off, or if income is transferred from the rich to the poor without reducing national income.

Pigou also introduced the idea of divergence between private and social costs (externalities) and suggested taxes and subsidies (Pigovian taxes) to correct them. Criticism: it assumes cardinal and comparable utility between persons, which is difficult to accept.
section-167: This criterion was given by Vilfredo Pareto. Conditions for Pareto optimality include efficiency in exchange (equal MRS for all consumers), efficiency in production (equal MRTS for all producers) and overall efficiency (MRS = MRT).

Limitations: There can be many Pareto-optimal points, each with a different distribution of income, so the criterion does not tell which is best. It also cannot judge changes where some gain and some lose, which is common in real policies.
section-168: Positive economics deals with 'what is' and avoids value judgments; normative economics deals with 'what ought to be' and involves them. For example, 'a tax increased prices' is positive, while 'the tax is unfair' is a value judgment.

Welfare economics cannot completely avoid value judgments because decisions about distribution and fairness require ethical choices. Robbins argued that interpersonal comparisons of utility are value judgments and are not scientific.
section-169: This criterion was proposed by Nicholas Kaldor (1939) and John Hicks (1940). It is a hypothetical compensation test: if the gains of the winners are greater than the losses of the losers, the change increases social welfare, whether or not compensation is actually paid.

It is used in cost-benefit analysis of projects such as dams and roads. Criticism: Scitovsky showed it can give contradictory results (Scitovsky paradox), and it ignores income distribution because losers may remain worse off if compensation is not paid.
section-170: The social welfare function was introduced by Abram Bergson (1938) and developed by Paul Samuelson. It is written as W = f(U1, U2, ..., Un), where U are the utilities of individuals. It allows ranking of different social states according to explicit value judgments.

Kenneth Arrow's Impossibility Theorem (1951) showed that no social welfare function based on individual preferences can satisfy all reasonable democratic conditions at the same time. Despite this, the concept helps clarify welfare choices and policy goals.
section-172: Perfect competition: Features include many buyers and sellers, homogeneous products, free entry and exit, perfect knowledge and mobility. The firm is a price taker with AR = MR. Equilibrium is at MC = MR with MC rising. In the short run the firm may earn supernormal profit, normal profit or losses; it shuts down if price falls below minimum AVC. In the long run, entry and exit ensure normal profit at minimum AC, so resources are used efficiently.

Monopoly: A single seller with no close substitutes and barriers to entry. AR slopes downward and MR lies below AR. Equilibrium is at MC = MR, and price exceeds MC. The monopolist can earn supernormal profits in the long run. Monopoly leads to higher price and lower output compared to perfect competition and causes deadweight loss.

Price discrimination: Charging different prices for the same product in different markets is possible when markets are separate and elasticities differ. Pigou's three degrees are first (perfect), second (by quantity blocks) and third (by market groups). It may be beneficial if it allows supply of services that would otherwise not be produced, such as railways.

Controlled and administered prices: Governments control prices of essential goods to protect consumers, and fix support prices to protect producers. Administered prices are fixed by firms or authorities. Such measures may cause shortages, black markets or fiscal burden if not well designed.
section-173: Monopolistic competition: Chamberlin's model has many firms selling differentiated products with selling costs. The demand curve slopes downward. In the short run, firms may earn supernormal profits; in the long run free entry reduces profits to normal, and the AR curve becomes tangent to AC above minimum AC, leading to excess capacity. Advertising and brand loyalty are important features.

Oligopoly: A few large firms dominate, decisions are interdependent and there may be collusion. Sweezy's kinked demand curve shows that rivals follow price cuts but not price rises, so demand is elastic above and inelastic below the current price. The discontinuity in MR explains price rigidity. Other forms include cartels and price leadership.
Duopoly: Two sellers, as analysed in Cournot's model, where each firm decides output assuming the other's output is constant; the equilibrium output lies between monopoly and competition.

Monopsony and bilateral monopoly: Monopsony is a single buyer, such as one employer in a town, who can pay less than the competitive price. Bilateral monopoly combines a single seller and a single buyer, and price is decided through bargaining within a range. These markets show that market power can exist on both sides of the market.
section-174: Marginal productivity theory: Factor prices equal their marginal revenue product under perfect competition. A firm hires a factor up to the point where MRP equals its price. The theory is criticised for its unrealistic assumptions.

Wages: The modern theory says wages are determined by demand for labour (derived demand based on productivity) and supply of labour (influenced by population, skills, mobility and preferences). Trade unions, minimum wage laws and collective bargaining also matter.

Rent: Ricardian differential rent arises from differences in fertility and location; scarcity rent arises from fixed supply; modern theory treats rent as surplus over transfer earnings; Marshall's quasi-rent is a short-run surplus on man-made capital equipment.

Interest and profit: Classical theory explains interest as the reward for saving, determined by saving and investment. Keynes's liquidity preference theory says interest is the reward for parting with liquidity, determined by money demand (transactions, precautionary and speculative motives) and money supply. Profit theories include Schumpeter's innovation theory, Hawley's risk theory and Knight's uncertainty theory. Factor-market equilibrium occurs where factor demand equals supply.
section-175: Meaning: Welfare economics is the normative branch of economics that evaluates whether economic arrangements make society better off. It considers efficiency in allocation and fairness in distribution.

Classical (Pigovian) welfare economics: Pigou measured economic welfare through national income and its distribution. Welfare rises if national income increases or if income is redistributed toward the poor. He identified externalities and proposed taxes and subsidies to correct them. His approach relied on cardinal and interpersonal utility comparisons.

Pareto criterion and new welfare economics: Pareto optimality requires efficiency in exchange, production and product mix. Because the Pareto criterion cannot judge changes with gainers and losers, Kaldor and Hicks proposed the compensation principle; Scitovsky pointed out its paradox and suggested a double test.

Social welfare function and value judgments: Bergson and Samuelson's social welfare function ranks social states using explicit value judgments. Arrow's Impossibility Theorem shows the difficulty of deriving a consistent social ordering from individual preferences. Amartya Sen extended welfare analysis through capability and social choice theory. Welfare economics thus guides public policy while recognising the role of ethics.
section-178: Adam Smith defined economics as the science of wealth, while Lionel Robbins defined it as the science of choice between unlimited ends and scarce means with alternative uses. Scarcity forces every economy to solve what, how and for whom to produce.

Demand depends on price, income, tastes and related goods; supply depends on price, costs, technology and taxes. The law of demand shows an inverse relation and the law of supply a direct relation with price, other things being equal. Equilibrium is where demand equals supply.
section-179: National income in India is estimated by the National Statistical Office using production, income and expenditure methods, with concepts such as GDP, GNP, NNP and per capita income. The budget may be balanced, surplus or deficit.

The Union Budget (Annual Financial Statement) is prepared by the Ministry of Finance, presented in Lok Sabha and passed through discussion, voting on demands for grants, the Appropriation Bill and the Finance Bill. Public revenue includes tax and non-tax revenue; public expenditure includes development and non-development spending.
section-180: India is a developing mixed economy with a large population, high dependence on agriculture for employment, a growing services sector, unemployment and inequality. Census 2011 showed a population of about 121 crore, decadal growth of 17.7 per cent and a sex ratio of 940.

Growth means increase in real GDP; development means improvement in quality of life measured by HDI and similar indicators. The economic reforms of 1991 (liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation) changed the direction of Indian economic policy.
section-182: Definitions: Adam Smith's wealth definition (1776) focused on the causes of national wealth; it was criticised as materialistic. Robbins's scarcity definition (1932) described economics as the science of choice; it is universal and positive but ignores welfare and growth.

Basic economic problems: What to produce (choice of goods), how to produce (choice of technique) and for whom to produce (distribution of output). These arise because resources are scarce and have alternative uses, and are illustrated by the production possibility curve.

Demand and supply: Demand is the quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at different prices; the law of demand is based on diminishing marginal utility, income and substitution effects. Supply is the quantity sellers offer; the law of supply is based on profit and rising cost. Interaction of demand and supply determines equilibrium price, and shifts in either curve change market outcomes.
section-183: National income: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year. GNP adds net factor income from abroad; NNP subtracts depreciation; national income is NNP at factor cost. Measurement uses the product, income and expenditure methods, and is affected by problems of informal activities and double counting.

Budget: Under Article 112, the Union Budget is the Annual Financial Statement. It may be balanced, surplus or deficit, and is divided into revenue and capital budgets. It is passed through presentation, general discussion, voting on demands, the Appropriation Bill and the Finance Bill.

Public revenue and expenditure: Revenue includes direct taxes (income tax, corporation tax), indirect taxes (GST, customs) and non-tax revenue (fees, dividends, interest). Expenditure includes defence, interest, subsidies, education, health and infrastructure. These tools of fiscal policy are used for growth, redistribution and stability.
section-184: Characteristics: India is a developing, mixed economy with a large population, predominance of agriculture in employment, rapid expansion of services, regional imbalance, income inequality and a large informal sector, along with a strong IT sector and growing digital economy.

Population: India's population was about 121 crore in 2011, with a decadal growth of 17.7 per cent and a sex ratio of 940. Population growth creates pressure on resources but a young workforce offers a demographic dividend if properly educated and employed.

Growth, development and reforms: Growth refers to rising real income, while development means improvement in health, education, equality and freedom. The 1991 reforms introduced liberalisation (removal of controls), privatisation (greater role for private sector and disinvestment) and globalisation (integration with the world economy). These reforms increased growth but also raised concerns about inequality and employment.
